Can a squatter take ownership of a Washington house?

Only by satisfying the adverse possession statutes over a long period. Washington sets a time limit on the owner's right to sue and has two statutes under which a long-term occupant can become the legal owner on defined conditions.

For an owner the issue is timing. The sections below separate an adverse possession claim from a trespass or unlawful detainer problem, which move on very different clocks.

Time needed for adverse possession

The general limit is ten years, and one route shrinks to seven years when the occupant has paper title and pays the taxes. Three statutes carry the rules:

  • RCW 4.16.020 gives ten years for actions to recover real property or its possession. An owner cannot bring the action unless the owner, a predecessor or a grantor was seized or possessed of the premises within ten years before the suit.
  • RCW 7.28.050 covers someone in actual, open and notorious possession for seven successive years who has a connected title in law or equity deducible of record. The owner must sue within seven years after possession was taken, or from the time the possessor acquires title if that is later.
  • RCW 7.28.070 covers someone in actual, open and notorious possession under claim and color of title made in good faith who stays seven successive years and pays all taxes legally assessed on the land in that time. That person is held to be the legal owner to the extent of the paper title.

The words that keep recurring are actual, open and notorious, and successive. Whether an occupant's facts fit them is for a court to decide, so an owner who suspects a claim should talk to a Washington attorney early.

Land and owners protected from these claims

Public land and land held by owners under certain legal disabilities are carved out. RCW 7.28.090 says the claim and color of title statutes do not reach lands of the United States or this state, school lands, or lands held for any public purpose. They also do not reach land where the holder of the adverse title is under eighteen or under a guardianship or conservatorship. That person must bring an action to recover the land within three years after the disability ends.

StatuteTimeCondition
RCW 4.16.020(1)10 yearsLimit on actions to recover real property or possession
RCW 7.28.0507 yearsActual, open and notorious possession with connected title deducible of record
RCW 7.28.0707 yearsClaim and color of title in good faith, plus payment of all taxes assessed
RCW 7.28.0903 years after disability endsOwner who is a minor or under guardianship or conservatorship

What happens when a claim is filed?

These disputes are heard in superior court, often through an action to quiet title. RCW 7.28.010 lets a person with a valid subsisting interest in real property and a right to possession recover it by action in the superior court of the proper county against the tenant in possession, and seek a judgment quieting or removing a cloud from the title. A person in actual possession can also bring a quiet title action against the unknown heirs of someone known to be dead.

RCW 7.28.083 adds money consequences for actions filed on or after July 1, 2012. A party who prevails against the record title holder, or a later purchaser from that holder, may be required to:

  • Reimburse part or all of the taxes and assessments the record holder paid during the possession, if proven by competent evidence.
  • Pay the county treasurer part or all of taxes levied after the claim was filed that remain unpaid when judgment is entered.

The court splits taxes between the land acquired and the land the titleholder keeps, as appears equitable and just. The prevailing party may also ask for costs and reasonable attorney fees, which the court may award in whole or in part. Both sides carry real cost risk once a claim reaches court.

Removing someone who has no right to be there

Washington uses the unlawful detainer statutes in chapter 59.12 RCW, and for a person who entered without permission the notice period is short. RCW 59.12.030(6) reaches a person who enters another's land without the owner's permission and without color of title and fails or refuses to leave after three days' written notice served as the statute requires. That person may also face criminal charges under chapter 9A.52 RCW.

Forcible detainer is a separate offense under RCW 59.12.020. It covers holding property by force or by menaces and threats of violence. It also covers entering at night or while the occupant is away and then refusing for three days after demand to give the property back to the former occupant, defined as someone in peaceable and undisturbed possession for the five days before the unlawful entry.

Once an unlawful detainer case is filed, RCW 59.12.090 lets the plaintiff apply for a writ of restitution restoring the property. The superior court clerk issues it, and it is returnable in twenty days. A writ requested before judgment needs a bond, set by the court, to cover costs and damages if the writ was wrongly obtained. A Washington attorney or the superior court clerk can tell you which papers your county requires.

Criminal trespass

Two degrees of criminal trespass can apply to someone who stays without right. First degree, RCW 9A.52.070, is knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building, and it is a gross misdemeanor. Second degree, RCW 9A.52.080, is knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in or upon the premises of another in circumstances that do not amount to first degree, and it is a misdemeanor.

Whether police or a prosecutor act depends on the facts, including whether the person claims permission, a lease or an ownership interest.

Selling an occupied house

Settle the occupancy question first, then sell. Keep a log of when you last visited, who has keys and what notices you sent, because dates matter under every statute above. Look up the tax records with the county treasurer, since payment of taxes is an element of a claim under RCW 7.28.070.

A house that is vacant, inherited, or occupied by someone you cannot move can still be sold to a cash buyer as is, and the closing agent can explain what the closing will need. Bring copies of any notices, court filings and the writ so the closing agent can see where things stand.

A short checklist to gather before you talk to a buyer, attorney or title company:

  • The last recorded deed and the legal description.
  • Dated copies of every notice you served and proof of service.
  • Any court filings, including a writ of restitution if one was issued.
  • Tax payment records for the parcel.

Frequently asked questions

How long must someone live in a house before claiming it in Washington?

The general limit for recovering real property is ten years (RCW 4.16.020). Seven years can apply when the occupant has color of title in good faith and pays all taxes (RCW 7.28.070), or has a connected record title (RCW 7.28.050).

Do squatters have to pay property taxes to win in Washington?

Under RCW 7.28.070, the occupant must pay all taxes legally assessed during the seven years. Under RCW 7.28.083, a court may also order a winning claimant to reimburse the record owner for taxes paid or pay unpaid taxes to the county treasurer.

How much notice does a trespasser get before an unlawful detainer case in Washington?

Someone who entered without permission and without color of title gets three days' written notice under RCW 59.12.030(6). If the person stays, the owner can file an unlawful detainer action in superior court.

Is trespassing a crime in Washington?

Yes. Knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building is first degree criminal trespass, a gross misdemeanor. Doing so on other premises is second degree, a misdemeanor (RCW 9A.52.070 and 9A.52.080).

Can a squatter claim public land in Washington?

No, not under the claim and color of title statutes. RCW 7.28.090 excludes land of the United States or this state, school lands, and lands held for any public purpose.

Washington Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Can a landlord end a tenancy to sell the house?

Only for a single-family residence, and only with at least 90 days' advance written notice. RCW 59.18.650 forbids a Washington landlord from evicting, refusing to continue a tenancy or ending a periodic tenancy except for causes the statute lists. One listed cause is that the owner elects to sell a single-family residence.

Electing to sell means making reasonable attempts within 30 days after the tenant leaves, at a minimum listing the home at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the multiple listing service. Two facts raise a rebuttable presumption that the owner never meant to sell: no listing within 30 days of the move-out, or, within 90 days after the move-out or the listing date (whichever is later), the owner takes the unit off the market, rents it to someone else or otherwise signals no intent to sell.

The sale ground is written for single-family homes. An owner of a duplex or a unit in a larger building should read the other listed causes and check with an attorney.

What happens to the lease when a rental house sells?

Because a tenancy can end only for a cause on the RCW 59.18.650 list, the lease and that list decide what a buyer inherits. A tenant on a fixed-term lease stays through the term unless landlord and tenant agree in writing to end it early and the tenant gets at least 60 days to move, under subsection (5).

So the house may come with a tenant in place. Three routes fit the statute:

  • Sell the property subject to the existing lease and rent.
  • Serve the 90-day notice for sale of a single-family residence and list the home once the tenant has moved.
  • Reach a written agreement with the tenant to end the tenancy early.

Any written notice under the cause list must be served as RCW 59.12.040 describes and must set out the facts behind the cause in enough detail for the tenant to respond.

The tenant's deposit when ownership changes

The deposit follows the tenancy. RCW 59.18.270 requires the landlord to put a security deposit promptly into a trust account at a Washington financial institution or with an escrow agent, give the tenant a written receipt, and tell the tenant in writing where the money is held. When the landlord's role passes to someone else during the tenancy, the funds move at the same moment to an equivalent trust account of the successor, who must promptly tell the tenant the new depository.

A foreclosure carries its own rule. If the home is foreclosed on and the deposit is not passed along, the former owner must promptly refund the full deposit to the tenant or face damages up to two times the deposit. The tenant's claim to deposit money also ranks ahead of the landlord's creditors, even when the money was mixed with other funds.

When you sell a tenant-occupied house, state the deposit amount in the purchase contract and confirm in writing who answers for it at closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Washington house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Returning the security deposit

The deadline is 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant has moved out. RCW 59.18.280 requires a full and specific statement of why any part is kept, with copies of estimates or paid invoices supporting damage charges, plus any refund owed. If the tenant simply left, the 30 days run from when the landlord learns of the abandonment. Handing over the papers or mailing them first class inside the 30 days meets the rule.

A landlord cannot keep deposit money for:

  • wear from ordinary use of the home;
  • carpet cleaning, unless the landlord documents wear beyond ordinary use;
  • repair or replacement of fixtures and appliances whose condition was not recorded on the move-in checklist;
  • more than the cost of repairing the damaged part, when only part of an item is damaged.

A landlord who misses the deadline owes the full deposit and loses the right to raise claims against it. A court may award up to two times the deposit for an intentional refusal, and whoever wins a deposit lawsuit recovers costs and reasonable attorneys' fees.

Showing the house to buyers

A landlord needs only one day's notice to show a rental to prospective or actual purchasers, while other entries need two. RCW 59.18.150 says that, outside an emergency or when it is impracticable, the landlord gives at least two days' written notice of intent to enter and enters only at reasonable times. The notice states the exact date and time, or the earliest and latest possible times, and a phone number the tenant can call to object or reschedule.

For a visit to exhibit the unit to buyers or tenants, the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent when at least one day's notice was given. The landlord may not exhibit the unit excessively or use entry to harass the tenant.

Either side that keeps breaking these rules after one written good-faith notice listing the date and time of the violation can be liable for up to $100 per violation, and the winner may recover costs and attorneys' fees. Put every notice in writing.

Rent increases and move-out notice

A rent increase needs at least 90 days' prior written notice to each affected tenant and cannot take effect before the rental agreement term ends, under RCW 59.18.140(3). Subsidized tenancies where rent depends on household income need only 30 days. A transitional rule covers some fixed-term leases signed or renewed before May 7, 2025 with more than 60 but fewer than 90 days left on that date: 60 days' notice.

A tenant ending a month-to-month tenancy gives written notice of 20 days or more before the end of a rental period under RCW 59.18.200(1). A member of the armed forces, or that member's spouse or dependent, may leave on shorter notice when orders for a permanent change of station or deployment do not allow 20 days.

An owner planning to demolish, substantially rehabilitate or change the use of a building owes tenants 120 days' written notice under the same section, which is worth knowing if you are weighing redevelopment before a sale.

Penalty for removing a tenant illegally

A landlord who removes a tenant, or causes removal, in violation of RCW 59.18.650 is liable for wrongful eviction. The tenant who wins is entitled to the greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs.

With that exposure, a seller with a tenant needs a clean paper trail: copies of written notices, proof of service, the listing date and the deposit accounting. If you are unsure which cause applies, ask the superior court clerk for the unlawful detainer forms, or hire a Washington landlord-tenant attorney before serving anything.

Notice periods in one place

SituationNotice or deadline
Owner elects to sell a single-family home90 days' written notice
Rent increase90 days (30 days for income-based subsidized tenancies)
Tenant ends month-to-month tenancy20 days or more, in writing
Entry to show to buyersOne day's notice
Deposit statement and refund30 days after move-out

Frequently asked questions

Does a new owner have to honor an existing Washington lease?

A tenancy can end only for a cause listed in RCW 59.18.650, and sale of a single-family residence is one, with 90 days' written notice. The deposit funds must transfer to the successor landlord under RCW 59.18.270.

How much notice must a Washington landlord give before showing a rental house to a buyer?

One day. RCW 59.18.150(6) bars a tenant from unreasonably refusing entry to exhibit the unit to purchasers once the landlord gave at least one day's notice. Other entries need two days' written notice.

Can a landlord raise rent on a tenant before selling?

Only with at least 90 days' prior written notice, and not before the rental agreement term ends. Subsidized income-based tenancies need 30 days under RCW 59.18.140(3).

Who is responsible for the tenant's deposit when the house is sold?

The deposit moves with the tenancy. The funds go to the successor landlord's trust account at the same time, and the successor promptly tells the tenant where the money is held.

What can a tenant recover if a landlord evicts without a valid cause?

The greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs, under RCW 59.18.650(4).

title: Washington Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Washington Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Washington
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Washington Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Washington Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Washington House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Washington?
We buy Washington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How many days of notice before an eviction?

The reason decides the length. For unpaid rent on a residential tenancy, the landlord serves a written pay-or-vacate notice and waits 14 days. For a lease violation other than rent, the wait is 10 days. For waste, a nuisance or an unlawful business, it is three days. RCW 59.12.030 sets those periods, and the cause list in RCW 59.18.650 ties back to them.

A tenant is liable for unlawful detainer on a rent or lease default only after the notice sits unanswered for the whole period. The notice always comes before any court filing.

Notice types and lengths

A Washington residential landlord generally cannot end a tenancy without one of the causes written into RCW 59.18.650, with narrow exceptions for certain fixed-term leases. These are the notice lengths that matter most to an owner trying to sell.

Reason for ending the tenancyWritten notice required
Unpaid rent14 days to pay or vacate
Lease or rule violation other than rent10 days to fix it or vacate
Waste, nuisance or unlawful activity3 days to quit
Owner or family moving in90 days
Owner selling a single-family home90 days
Home certified or condemned as unfit to live in30 days
Tenant shares a kitchen or bath with the owner20 days
Demolition, major rehab or change of use120 days

What the 14-day pay or vacate notice must contain

The form in RCW 59.18.057 has to be followed substantially as written. It breaks out unpaid rent, utilities and other recurring charges month by month, shows the total due, and names the place where payment goes. It also tells the tenant to pay as the rental agreement directs or by a nonelectronic method such as a cashier's check or money order.

Any payment is applied first to the total on the notice, and the notice says so. It also points the tenant to help: the Attorney General's rental assistance website, the Eviction Defense Screening Line for qualifying low-income renters, the Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline, dispute resolution centers for low-cost mediation, and the right to a court interpreter.

  • Itemize each month and each charge category on its own line.
  • Include a payment address and the owner or landlord name.
  • Date the notice so the days can be counted from service.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Washington house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Serving the notice

RCW 59.12.040 permits three methods. One is handing the tenant a copy in person. A second applies when the tenant is out: leave a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the home and mail another copy to the residence. The third is for when the tenant's whereabouts are unknown or no suitable person can be found. Then the landlord posts the notice in a conspicuous place, hands a copy to anyone living there, and mails a copy.

Mail service is complete the day the copy goes into a Washington mailbox with postage paid, but five more days must go by before a case can be started on that notice. Every termination notice also has to state the date by which the tenant must leave or, where relevant, comply.

Causes under RCW 59.18.650 demand more. Those notices are served the same way and must lay out the facts the landlord knew at the time in enough detail for the tenant to prepare a response.

Ending a tenancy because the house is being sold

It is allowed, but only on the terms of RCW 59.18.650(2)(e). A tenant who stays after the owner elects to sell a single-family residence can be removed if the landlord gave at least 90 days' advance written notice of the date possession ends. The owner is treated as electing to sell by making reasonable attempts within 30 days after the tenant moves out, at a minimum listing the home at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the multiple listing service.

The law presumes, subject to rebuttal, that the owner never meant to sell when the home is not listed within 30 days of the move-out. The same presumption applies if, within 90 days after the move-out or the listing date, whichever is later, the owner takes the house off the market, rents it to someone new or otherwise shows no intent to sell.

A fixed-term lease cannot be cut short on this ground. Subsection (5) permits that only with the tenant's written consent and at least 60 days for the tenant to vacate.

Penalty for removing a tenant illegally

A landlord who removes a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 is liable for wrongful eviction. A winning tenant can recover the greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs. This reaches any removal that breaks the section, so an owner who wants a vacant house for sale should follow every notice and court step.

An indigent tenant in an eviction case can also have a court-appointed attorney, depending on available funding.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Washington houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If a tenant will not leave a house that is for sale

Count the notice period from the service date, keep proof of how the notice was delivered, and file nothing in superior court until the period is over. Unlawful detainer for unpaid rent applies when the tenant neither pays nor leaves in time. A lease violation can be cured within 10 days of service.

Before you commit to a sale date, add up the timeline. The 90-day sale notice comes first, and a court case follows if the tenant stays. A signed move-out agreement is another route: for a fixed-term lease the statute allows an early end when the tenant consents in writing and gets at least 60 days to leave. A lawyer or the county superior court clerk can confirm local filing steps.

What to bring if you visit the clerk or an attorney:

  • The lease and any written amendments.
  • A copy of the notice you served and the date and method of service.
  • The rent ledger showing each month and charge.
  • Your listing agreement or sale plans, if the sale is the reason for the notice.

Keep a folder with each notice, the proof of service, the lease and the rent ledger. A buyer, a title company or a judge will want to see them, and they help a cash buyer price the house as is without waiting on the tenant's schedule.

Frequently asked questions

How long is a Washington eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Fourteen days for a residential tenancy. The landlord serves a written pay-or-vacate notice, and if the tenant neither pays nor leaves within 14 days of service, an unlawful detainer case can be filed.

Can a Washington landlord evict without a reason?

Generally no. RCW 59.18.650 bars eviction, refusal to continue a tenancy or ending a periodic tenancy except for listed causes. Narrow exceptions let a landlord end certain leases of six months or longer at their end with 60 days' written notice.

How much notice does a Washington landlord give to sell the house?

At least 90 days in writing for a single-family residence, and the owner has to list the home within 30 days after the tenant moves out. Otherwise the law presumes the owner never meant to sell.

How must a Washington eviction notice be delivered?

By handing it to the tenant, by leaving a copy with a suitable person and mailing another, or, when neither works, by posting it, giving a copy to a resident and mailing one. Mail service adds five days before a case can start.

What is the penalty for an illegal eviction in Washington?

A winning tenant recovers the greater of actual damages or three times the monthly rent, plus attorneys' fees and court costs, under RCW 59.18.650(4).
